speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move the following motion:

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE EFFECTS OF RAIL STRIKE ON ISOLATED COMMUNITIES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order
43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity dealing with the many effects the rail strike has had and is having across this country, in particular, the effects of the rail strike on isolated communities all across the country. I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Mal-peque (Mr. MacLean):
That the government take immediate steps to provide vital services to alleviate inconveniences suffered by travellers on our island provinces, to facilitate movement of feed grain to livestock producers, to provide vital food supplies to isolated northern communities and to ensure that the health and welfare of all Canadian citizens are not affected in any way by the detrimental consequences of this national strike.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED MISTREATMENT OF CREW MEMBERS OF "GREENPEACE III"-SUGGESTED DEMAND FOR APOLOGY FROM FRANCE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the denial of the government of France of any mistreatment or beating of the crew members of the Greenpeace III, and in view of the production of factual photographs to the contrary, I ask leave of the House under the terms of Standing Order 43 to move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan):
That this House instruct the Prime Minister to demand a public apology from the government of France and to demand that those involved in this assault be brought to justice and that compensation be paid to those injured in this unprovoked assault which took place on one of our ships in international waters.

That the matter of beef and pork export controls be referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture for study and report.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
speechtext:
Pursuant to special order made earlier today, Mr. Munro (Hamilton East), seconded by Mr. Davis (Capilano), moves:
That Bill C-217, an act to provide for the resumption and continuance of operations of railways and for the settlement of the disputes with respect to terms and conditions of employment between railway companies and their employees, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as members of this House, I am sure, are well aware,
August 30, 1973

the bill which is now before them concerns the government's legislative proposals respecting the resumption of rail services. The reasons for these proposals are, I believe, equally well known. The suspension of railway operations and subsidiary services which began regionally on July 26 and nationally on August 23 has resulted in widespread economic loss to the extent that the welfare of the nation has become imperilled. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has indicated, it is essential to the interests of the people of Canada and the welfare of our nation that railway operations be resumed immediately.
Before examining these legislative proposals in some detail it would be appropriate for me to outline to hon. members the sequence of events leading up to the recall of parliament. First, however, I would refer to the parties involved in the present, three separate disputes: these are the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railway companies along with other short-line companies while, on the union side, the associated non-operating railway unions, the United Transportation Union and division No. 4, Railway Employees, department of AFL-CIO, representing the various shopcraft unions. In all, the disputes involve approximately 91,000 employees across the country.
The current strike involving the non-operating unions stems from unsuccessful attempts to renegotiate a collective agreement that expired on December 31 last. Disputes involving the shopcrafts and the United Transportation Union also result from agreements unrenewed since the same date, but in these disputes no strike action has as yet been taken.
In all cases early mediation assistance was sought, and this my department provided in full measure. With regard to the dispute involving the non-operating unions, failure to negotiate an agreement after intensive mediation led to the appointment of a conciliation board chaired by Mr. Justice F. Craig Munroe of the Supreme Court of British Columbia. The board report, which was released to the parties on July 13, recommended the following wage increases: effective January 1, 1973, 30 cents an hour or 8.5 per cent of the basic rate; effective January 1, 1974, an increase of 5 per cent on the rates in effect as of December, 1973; effective July 1, 1974, an increase of 3 per cent on the rates in effect as of June, 1974.
Subsequently, the union announced its intention to conduct selective strikes. The first such strike occurred on July 26, and others followed in other regions of the country. On August 7, I appointed Judge Alan B. Gold, of Montreal, as mediator and he met with the parties continuously over the next 11 days to try to bring about a settlement. The non-operating unions began their national rail strike on August 23. Since then I made a further effort and, with the assistance of experienced mediators in the department, explored every avenue to find a solution short of recalling parliament.
On August 27, after a complete review of the situation with my officials, I advised the Prime Minister and my colleagues that, in the public interest, parliament be recalled to restore railway service. With regard to the dispute involving the shopcraft unions, a conciliation
Railway Operations Act
board was established on June 26, 1973, after the union membership had rejected a negotiated settlement. The board's majority report, which was received on August 13, proposed a wage increase of 8.25 per cent effective January 1, 1973; an increase of 6V2 per cent on January 1, 1974, based on wages in effect as of December, 1973; and an increase of 1V4 per cent as of July 1, 1974, based on wages in effect in June, 1974.
Two days after the release of the board's report, the president of division No. 4 advised that his negotiating committee, representing 22,000 employees, had rejected the majority report. The shopcraft employees were in a position to strike on August 21 and are presently conducting a strike vote, with the results to be known about September 10. With regard to the dispute involving the United Transportation Union, which represents some
14,000	trainmen, conductors and yardmen, a conciliation board was established on May 29, 1973, chaired by R. A. Gallagher, Q.C., of Winnipeg. The board held hearings in Montreal on July 25, 26 and 27 and the report was received on August 24. The board report contained no recommendation on wages. At present, the general chairmen of the UTU are considering the board report and would be in a legal strike position on September 1.
This brief resume, while by no means a complete analysis of the events backgrounding the situation facing us today, does, I think, provide some useful perspective. Many are the opinions that can be ventured, many are the criticisms that can be levelled; but at this juncture, to no avail. Suffice to say that this strike has occurred despite the most sustained and painstaking efforts at mediation; that the task now before parliament is to restore rail operations and allied services and to provide a process that can fairly and equitably settle, finally, the terms and conditions of employment of the employees involved for the years 1973 and 1974.
The proposed legislation now before hon. members may be cited as the Maintenance of Railway Operations Act,
1973.	Basically, the provisions deal with the three disputes individually. However, there are a number of provisions that are common to all, and with hon. members' consent I will enumerate those major provisions affecting all three groups. Firstly, in so far as the resumption of services is concerned, in this most vital area the act states that every company and every employee shall resume work, or continue work, as the case may be, forthwith upon the coming into force of this legislation. This order invalidates and overrides any prior authorization that may have been given to take strike action. The act also forbids any railway company personnel to refuse to permit any striking employee from resuming work duties forthwith. Further, no such striking employee may in any way be disciplined for having been on strike.
Secondly, the act provides for the extension of all collective agreements pertaining to the three groups, with certain important amendments to the agreements which I will explain in a moment. In all cases, the extension will be from January 1, 1973, to the day on which any new collective agreements come into effect, or December 31,
1974,	whichever is the earlier. This extension, and the amendments, are binding.

August 30, 1973
Railway Operations Act
Thirdly, the act orders all railway companies and unions involved to resume negotiations forthwith with a view to settling matters presently in dispute. It further orders that they negotiate in good faith and make every reasonable effort to conclude a new settlement. Any new settlement, it should be noted, can in no event expire before December 31, 1974.
Fourthly, the act empowers me, as minister, to appoint mediators in the reopened negotiations. In addition, the governor in council may, on my recommendation, appoint an arbitrator whether or not a mediator has been appointed.
These four areas that 1 have mentioned are common to all three groups. I will now deal with those provisions that affect the groups individually. First may I deal with the non-operating employees. The amendments to the nonoperating employees contract are as follows, as set out in this bill: an increase of 30 cents per hour effective January 1, 1973; an increase of 5 per cent effective January 1, 1974; and an increase of 3 per cent effective July 1, 1974. In each case the increase refers to each hourly basic rate of wages. It will be quickly realized, I am sure, that these increases are those recommended by the chairman of the conciliation board.

Shoperaft employees are the next group. The amendments to the shoperaft employees contract are as follows, and are identical with those recommended by the report of the conciliation board: an increase of 8!4 per cent effective January l, 1973; an increase of 6Vi per cent effective January 1, 1974; an increase of IV2 per cent effective July 1, 1974. In each case the increase refers to each hourly basic rate of wages.
The third group is the railway operating employees. The amendments to the railway operating employees contract are as follows: an increase of 8!4 per cent effective January 1, 1973; an increase of 6V1 per cent effective January 1, 1974; and an increase of IV2 per cent effective July 1, 1974. In each case the increase refers to each hourly basic rate of wages or mileage basic rate. I should emphasize that the wage increases for all employees involved in the three disputes, which are provided for in this act, are minimal. Any subsequent negotiated wages settlements or decisions reached through arbitration can in no case reflect wage increases which would be lower than those stated in this act.
Now I would like to speak about pension plans. Hon. members are well aware I am sure, of the significance of the question of pensions and their costs throughout the negotiations. I understand that a number of members of all parties have received representations on this subject. Agreement with all unions bargaining with the railway companies on the matter of pension benefits was reached on March 16. It should be emphasized that pension gains made by all the unions acting in unison are a major accomplishment in the history of railway negotiations.
However, there has been some controversy concerning the railways' cost estimates of such benefits, estimates which are alleged to be exaggerated. I have come to the conclusion that harmony will not prevail among railway employees unless this cost question is aired and answered

by an independent inquiry. Consequently, I have appointed an industrial inquiry commission, pursuant to part V of the Canada Labour Code, to estimate the cost of the negotiated settlement relating to pensions and comment on any differences between its cost estimate and that of the railway companies. I might add that today I appointed John Deutsch to be the industrial inquiry commissioner to conduct this inquiry.

In making any recommendation to the governor in council regarding the whole matter of an arbitrator, to which I have referred, I intend to recommend that in addition to the matters that would be referred to him he should consider the results of the inquiry into pension costing that I have previously mentioned. This important proviso will, I am sure, meet with the fullest approval of the employee unions concerned in these disputes.
It is obvious, I think, to all members that the question of job security, which is of grave concern to all rail workers, is one of those items that would be considered during the mediation process, or by arbitration. I think this should be underlined and noted by the employees and the unions concerned.
Before attempting to answer any questions there may be concerning the legislation that I have outlined, I should like to respectfully reiterate a statement made by the Prime Minister when he announced the recall of parliament on August 27. He said:
In recalling parliament our first priority will be the immediate restoration of rail service throughout Canada. I also want to assure the railway unions and managements that the government will continue to respect their interests.
I am satisfied that both these priorities will be achieved by the legislative proposals and the inquiry commission whose appointment I have just announced. I might add, in terms of some of the concern that has been expressed by the workers with reference to the cost of living, that the increases now being implemented-and of course this will involve retroactive payments to all those concerned back to January 1 of this year-can be taken into account by any arbitrator who might be appointed with reference to this dispute.

This government, Mr. Speaker, in spite of repeated requests from the House, continues to ignore the recommendations of the Woods committee report which was presented to them in December, 1968. They ignored the major recommendations of that report, recommendations which addressed themselves to the problems I have outlined for negotiating strikes in essential services.
Our party has put forward a proposal based on many of the recommendations contained in the Woods report. We have said we would establish an essential services disputes commission which would define essential services and prescribe the procedure for settling disputes within these essential services. Accordingly, our party endorsed the recommendations made to the government back in December, 1968, in the Woods committee report for the establishment of a public interest disputes commission. This commission would advise whether particular services are essential, set out procedures for resolving differences where the public interest is threatened and, where it is unsuccessful, would report to the government for possible parliamentary action to end a strike or lockout. That is the kind of leadership this country needs.
There can be no doubt that the present rail strike constitutes a national crisis. We meet in an air of crisis. Neither can we doubt the fact that this government had ample warning. It knew this strike was coming, but did nothing about it. As a result, grain shipments have been stopped: this could have long-term, serious consequences to our wheat markets and to the economy of western Canada. Beef and produce are rotting on rail sidings. Ferry services to our two island provinces have been disrupted, stranding thousands of tourists in Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia.
What is even more important, serious food shortages are developing in many parts of the country. This is especially true in my own province, Newfoundland, which depends on the railways for most of its food, which has to be imported from the mainland. Mr. Speaker, the government had ample warning. The question is: Why did they not act? What are the facts? They are as follows: negotiations for a new contract began on November 1, 1972. The government knew that the contract was expiring, or would expire at the end of that year. On December 21, 1972, federal mediation was required. On February 16 those negotiations collapsed and the assistant deputy minister of labour was called in.
On March 17 the minister was requested to establish a conciliation board, and the board was set up on May 16, 1973. Early in July the reports of the conciliation board were officially submitted to the minister. At this point I submit the minister should have intervened personally, but he did not. Instead, the government adjourned parliament, knowing full well that there was little or no hope for a negotiated settlement without government and parliamentary intervention. So we end up with a costly rail strike. Finally, on August 7, the minister appointed Judge Alan Gold of Montreal as federal mediator. Why did the minister not intervene? When he intervened, it was too late. When the minister finally decided to intervene, we were not witnessing rotating or selective strikes; we were witnessing a full-blown, national railway strike-and then it was too late.
We were all witnessess to the minister's performance. We all saw on television the charade and theatrics played by the minister in the hours leading up to the Prime Minister's announcement last Monday. There he was, with his collar open, running from car to car and from hotel to hotel, trying to make us believe that he was trying to bring about a settlement of this dispute when he knew that no such settlement at that point in time was possible. Just last night the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Turner) was quoted on the CBC national news as having said that the railways did not negotiate in good faith; they held firm, knowing that the government would have to intervene.

Certainly, Mr. Speaker, the railways did not bargain in good faith; that is a fact. Whatever else can be said about the railways, this can be said of them: they had their hands tied by the Minister of Transport and his intemperate outburst in western Canada. I say that the railways have a lot to answer for in this whole affair. Parliament has been denied, by this government, the traditional right to examine the Canadian National annual report in committee. That right has been denied to the members of this House for the past two years. What does the government and the railway have to hide? For the past two years we have been denied the right to a full examination of the budget and finances relating to the CNR and, as a consequence, no auditors have been appointed.
How can the government expect parliament to vote on the matter of wage increases when the financial position of the CNR, a Crown corporation, is unknown? Whatever can be said for Canadian Pacific-and I understand that
August 30, 1973

the CN usually falls into line with their thinking-there is no doubt in anybody's mind that we have a right and, indeed, a responsibility to have the management of this Crown corporation come before a committee of parliament and give a full accounting to the representatives of the people. If the CN annual report for the current year had been referred to a committee of this House, in keeping with past customs and practices, and if we had been given full and ample opportunity to examine in detail the CN financing bill, as we are entitled to do, we would have been in a much better position today to assess properly the attitude taken by the major employers, the CPR and CNR, in this dispute.
According to the evidence that is available, the railway companies are not too badly off. We understand that gross revenue for the CPR is up considerably. We know that the railways have had a good year. Last year, CN's profit was up to $48.3 million, their best year ever. Based on an average hourly wage of $3.64, a 10 per cent increase to all three union groups-that is, the non-ops, the shopcrafts and the trainmen-representing a total of 90,000 workers would cost a minimum of $68.1 million per year. That may seem like a lot, but when you think in terms of a gross revenue of $1,405.8 million for CN in 1972, that is not so much after all. Only then can one get a much truer perspective. We can better appreciate the human problems involved if we bring those figures down to human terms and think of the difference that an increase from $3 to $3.30 per hour will make to a man with a family, to a man who is bringing home the food, or bringing home the bacon as we say in Newfoundland. Of course, he cannot afford bacon today. Nevertheless, that is the issue. That is what this government fails to understand, because it is a government without heart.
Finally, it is unfortunate that this legislation will also cover the shopcrafts and trainmen, even though they have not exhausted the full process of the existing law with regard to a strike vote and final mediation attempts. Though the shopcrafts were much better off than their brothers in the non-ops, they had not had a change in their base rate for many years; and while they have rejected the report of the conciliation board, they have not yet taken their strike vote. Consequently, I am not too proud about what we are doing with respect to the shopcrafts union in this bill.
The United Transportation Union, or the trainmen, are faced with railway company demands to reduce train crews. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour knows what that means. If the railway companies get their way, it will mean a reduction in the work force of some 2,000 men. More important, Sir, this will create very serious operating hazards, and the hon. member for London East who is Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour knows this full well.
We need new ways of resolving disputes which arise within federal jurisdiction. There is no doubt in my mind that public interest sectors under federal jurisdiction, such as the railways, have not kept pace with all other aspects of society. They have not kept pace with their fellow workers because they are, by the very nature of their work, classed as essential. They know full well that if they resort to the ultimate protection the law affords

them-that is, the right to strike-parliament will be recalled and they will be legislated back to work. As a consequence, they have fallen behind. We must start to find new ways to improve the bargaining process in industries under federal jurisdiction. By example, through that bargaining process throughout the country, we must find ways to make certain that bargaining takes place well in advance of the expiry date of a contract.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to spend any more time on things which may have been said by spokesmen for the official opposition. Our appeal is to the government as well as to the members of the official opposition with respect to the bill which is now before us.
My hon. friends and I agree, of course, that a national rail strike causes extreme hardship in many sections of

the country and that it is very deleterious to the economy as a whole. We, of course, agree that parliament has a duty to the people of Canada and to the public interest, and that there comes a point in a strike such as a national railway strike at which members of parliament must take the responsibility of making certain that rail operations are resumed so that the harm, the difficulties, the hardship caused by the strike are ended.
To say this, however, is to accept only half of our responsibility as members of parliament-only half of the responsibility of parliament and of the government of Canada. It is not enough for us to say to more than 90,000 Canadians that their normal democratic rights are to be taken away, and to order them to go back to work on the basis of a settlement such as is contained in the bill before us, a settlement which is clearly inadequate and unjust.

Therefore, in spite of our anxiety, which is as great as that felt by members in any quarter of the House, to see the rail strike come to an end, we cannot accept the bill as introduced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). It was suggested by the minister in his speech that the wage settlements proposed in the bill were minima. As a matter of fact, I suppose it was a slip of the tongue; he said they were minimal. He was right; they are minimal. But the word in the written version of the speech was "minima". The rest would be done by somebody else, by a mediator or an arbitrator. It was suggested by another speaker this afternoon that parliament would not negotiate an agreement, that this must be left to someone else. I think we should face the truth and acknowledge that this is precisely what parliament is doing; what we are doing is making amendments to the collective agreement of the railway employees involved.
There is provision in the bill for some things to be decided elsewhere, but we all know what will happen. I say to the minister that the proposal for further mediation which the bill contains is, to put it mildly, fatuous. Negotiations have gone on for nine months. There have been four mediators-Mr. Gibbons, Mr. Kelly from the minister's department, Judge Gold, and the minister himself. What more could be done by way of mediation? I say to the minister, because I have some experience in these matters, that once this bill passes and the men and women are ordered back to work-assuming for the moment that they obey the order-all the pressure on the companies, all the pressure on the mediator or arbitrator is gone. Perhaps after that some improvements will be made here and there, but no real justice will be forthcoming for the workers involved.
The minister said the wage proposal contained in the bill is the one suggested or recommended by the board. I am sure he knew this was a mistake. It was not recommended by the board, because there was no board report. It was a settlement proposed by the chairman of the board, Mr. Justice Munroe of the Supreme Court of British Columbia. What is more significant is that the proposal which the minister's bill contains represents the latest offer of the railway companies, the one they made just two days ago when they said they were prepared to accept the Munroe recommendation. So what the government is
August 30, 1973

asking parliament to do is to order the men and women now on strike, and those who contemplate going on strike, to accept the latest railway offer. If that is not serving the railways, I do not know what is.

There are seldom real negotiations between the railways and employees' organizations. Someone mentioned the fact that there have been three parliamentary actions in the last 23 or 25 years. That is true. None the less, I think we ought to recognize that while there was a strike and parliamentary action in 1950, there were settlements in 1952, 1954, 1956, 1958, 1960, 1962 and 1964, and it was not until 1966 that there was another disruption. Let us not say that the situation has been awful over the years, because both sides have behaved very well since 1966 when there were two negotiated settlements before the difficulties which have occurred at this time.
The reason for the difficulties are twofold. I am grateful to the hon. member for St. John's East who quoted words I uttered in 1966. I did not bother to look up my words of wisdom, as I often find when I look at them seven years later that they sound a great deal less wise than when I first uttered them. Of course that was the situation in 1966, and that is still the situation today; the rising cost of living and the non-action of the government to deal with it
Railway Operations Act
in some effective way has added fuel to the negotiating fires. The fact is that the railway employees have fallen behind lamentably. They have validated their case by facts which have not been controverted except by misstatements by the railways, to which I may come if I have time.
As of January 1, 1972, I think all of the employees covered by this bill, certainly the non-ops, received an increase of 7 per cent in their wages. The increase in the cost of living from January, 1972, to July, 1973, has been 10 per cent. They are now 3 per cent behind the position they held when they got their last increase on January 1, 1972. They are already 3 per cent behind. I suggest to the. minister that the roughly 8 per cent he proposes for the first year of the agreement, which is an increase of 30 cents an hour, will do no more for those employees than cover the likely increase in the cost of living in 1973-if it does that. I suggest the increase in the cost of living for this year will be between 7 per cent and 8 per cent, or higher.
What the minister is asking the employees to do is to kindly go back to work on the basis of the wage arrangement in this bill which takes them not one step forward but leaves them in exactly the same position they were in nine months ago.

When I was able to practise law, before I was elected to parliament, I acted for the employees in various capacities, but when I was elected to parliament I felt there might easily be a conflict of interest if I continued to do so. During those years from 1952 to 1962, the area of comparability used related to the durable goods industry and there was an average developed between employees in the durable goods industry and non-operating employees so far as wages are concerned.
Let us consider the situation in respect of the traditional non-operating employee group, including not only those now covered by the first part of the bill but also those covered by the second part, namely the shopcrafts employees. I do not want to be technical about it, but I merely want to point out that in June, 1973, the average hourly earnings of durable goods industry employees was $4.17. We built the CPR on the basis of the millions of dollars and millions of acres given by the people of this country. That company has built an immense economic empire without any risk. In 1972 the CPR increased its profits over 1971 by 27 per cent. In the first half of 1973 it increased its profits by 53 per cent over the first half of 1972. This is the company which we say ought to have the advantage of this parliament sending its employees back to work on the basis of this inadequate settlement. I say no.
The fact is that this poverty-stricken company received in subsidies, in 1972, more than it paid in taxes in 1972. It received in subsidies $30,367,000. That is the rail operation. I am not talking about the various gifts given by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to Cominco and other subsidiaries. The CPR rail operation received subsidies amounting to $30,367,000 in 1972, and indicated in its 1972 annual report a tax liability of $30,200,000.
The fact is that out of that there is a deferred tax of $1Vi million, so that in 1972 this poverty-stricken railway company received about $2 million more out of the public treasury than it put into it in taxes. Yet we are told that this company is entitled to some consideration by this government and by this parliament. This corporate welfare bum had, as of December, 1972, deferred taxes totalling $143 Vi million. Those are taxes from the people of Canada, and that is an interest-free loan to the CPR. It is no wonder I have always had the view that the Canadian Pacific Railway should be nationalized and that we would take a big step forward if we did that very shortly.
There is no validity in any argument by the railways that they do not have the ability to pay any legitimate and just increase to which the employees are entitled. I want to make it very clear that I do not agree with the statement made by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) made an intemperate statement in Calgary, that there would be a freeze on freight rates for 18 months. He did not impose it, but said to the railways that there should be such a freeze. I would ask the hon. member who spoke previously to ask the Conservative Premier of Alberta whether he would agree that the Minister of Transport was wrong.
The railway companies, particularly if you take their entire empires, are well able to pay a decent wage to their employees. I say that this House ought not to pass any legislation that does not give them a decent wage and makes at least some advance. However, the Minister of Labour did not bring in a bill which even covers Mr. Justice Munroe's recommendation. It covers only the matter of wages. Mr. Justice Munroe made recommendations with regard to job security, which is of great importance to the non-ops in particular.
What hon. members and what the people of Canada, if I may say so without presumption, ought to realize is that the work force of the railways in Canada has been cut in half in the last 20 years. It has gone down by 37 per cent in the last 15 years. The work done by the railways, with half the force they had 20 years ago, is two or three times as great as the work done 20 years ago. With half the work

force, and therefore having to pay relatively half the wage bill they had to pay 20 years ago, their productivity is two or three times as high as it was 20 years ago. I simply ask, are not the employees of the railways entitled to part of that productivity increase? This productivity increase was created not only by additional capital, although that played a part, and not only by the capital to buy new equipment, although that played a part; it was also created by the employees of the railways doing their work in a better or newer fashion, in a better trained fashion. They made some contribution to the increased productivity of the railways; and I ask the members of this House, are they not entitled to part of that productivity increase?
The Weldon recommendation would give them no more than about 3 per cent above the increase in the cost of living. Surely they are entitled to part of the productivity increase of more than 6 per cent which annually has taken place on the railways. There are some other details with which some of my colleagues will deal. The Weldon formula suggests that if we are to do justice to the people concerned, we should have a more stringent guarantee that everyone will be employed if this strike ends and when it ends, and that there will not be the usual days of delay before some people are called back.
As a matter of fact, in the case of the shopcraft workers and members of the UTU, the bill does not provide any job security when the strike ends except for those who are on strike, and since none of them has been on strike but many have been laid off because of the non-ops strikes, there is no job security for those who were laid off and did not strike. The bill should contain a provision that the unions have argued for, namely, for job security.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have about six or seven minutes left. Let me take a minute or two to deal with that matter. I have said, and I say again, that in the last 20 years there has been a cut in half of the work force on the railways, and in the last 15 years a cut of 37 per cent. That has meant a reduction of a good many jobs. In 1957 I was involved in the dispute between the firemen and the CPR with regard to firemen on the diesel engines. The firemen were not very happy, but we finally settled the dispute, despite their unhappiness, on the basis that no firemen with more than two or three years service would be laid off-I forget the exact details-and that attrition would take care of the reduction in jobs. It took 10 or 12 years to achieve that, but finally it was adopted.
According to the report of Professor Weldon which gives the details on this, what the unions have asked for and what Dr. Weldon has recommended with regard to job security is that any person with four years' service should not be laid off. The unions have referred to two years' service; Dr. Weldon proposes this with regard to four years' service. Anyone with four years' service or more should not be laid off by the railway companies, and attrition will take care of the reduction in jobs. In this the unions have taken a step far in advance of any they have taken before. The unions, as well as Dr. Weldon, propose that if a job becomes redundant, the employee who has over four years' service should be given an opportunity to relocate, to retrain, to take another job in some other locality, and if he refuses the railways will be free to

According to the Weldon report-I have known Dr. Weldon for many years and I am certain he would not state anything the factual accuracy of which he was not convinced about-30 per cent of the employees in the non-ops group, and here I am referring only to the non-ops group on the railways, have less than four years' service, and there has been a rate of attrition every year of about 4 or 5 per cent through ordinary resignations and deaths. So, as it were, the railways have a 35 per cent cushion in dealing with job security for the remaining 65 per cent of their employees who have had more than four years' service. It is obviously an ample cushion, and it would not cost the railways a penny to provide this job security.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, to the minister, to the Prime Minister and to members of the government that in my discussions with the non-operating employee leaders-and I have had many of them over the last few days, and indeed few weeks-the fact has been underlined that job security is a very important issue for the people concerned. In fact, it is of great importance to everyone in this rather uncertain and difficult world.
Despite what I have said about our anxiety to see resumed rail and other operations related to the railways, I must say to you, Sir, that we cannot support the bill as presently presented to this parliament.

I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for his enlightened comments but I am sure he appreciates the difficulty of the Chair in respect of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis).
There are very few amendments that can be moved on second reading. Hon. members know what they are: they are the traditional amendments such as the three months' hoist, the six months' hoist and the referral of the subject matter of a bill to a committee. There is also the reasoned amendment. It is somewhat difficult for the Chair to make rulings in a general way as to which amendments, which so-called reasoned amendments, are acceptable, but it is fundamental in understanding reasoned amendments that members should be aware that such amendments must attempt to indicate why one proposes to vote against the bill. There must be something in a proposed so-called reasoned amendment which indicates why the mover of the amendment will vote against the bill.
In this particular instance it seems to me that what the hon. member is doing, rather than what I have just suggested, is to propose an entirely new proposition. subtopic: GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION-SUGGESTED MOVING OF SOME SERVICES TO ALBERTA
speechtext:
On April 5 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to explain the government's policy on decentralization of government services. I asked him what the policy of the government was, and he said decentralization had already been brought about. That was certainly not the fullest of answers. It was also somewhat premature. In the interim, of course, we have witnessed the Western Economic Opportunities Conference in Calgary which emphasized that the west should share more intimately in the decision-making process.
The government has sought to give the impression that it is taking decentralization seriously. Thus, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) has announced a decentralization program in accordance with which the proportion of departmental staff in the capital has been reduced from 70 per cent to 30 per cent and staff at regional offices expanded from 30 per cent to 70 per cent of the total.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION-SUGGESTED MOVING OF SOME SERVICES TO ALBERTA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION-SUGGESTED MOVING OF SOME SERVICES TO ALBERTA
speechtext:
The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) has outlined plans to make more purchases from regions which are distant from the national capital. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is increasing the resources and responsibilities of regional offices, especially in counselling programs for small business. The Royal Canadian Mint extension is being located in Winnipeg. The concept of decentralization of federal government activity, as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) tells us, is nothing more and nothing less than a concept of equality. "It is essential that every Canadian know that the nation's business is nationwide", the minister says. And I agree.
One might think that with all this activity the need for decentralization is being met. But it is not. Decentralization means more than a slight shifting of the federal payroll out from Ottawa. It means stopping the shocking proliferation of government buildings here in Ottawa as indicated by the plan to take over huge amounts of commercial space south of Wellington Street. It also means bringing the decision-making process closer to the people, and this implies essentially that regional interests will become a priority of the federal government.
For too long we have silently watched government grow and grow to the point at which we are now one of the most overgoverned people on earth. The joint parliamentary committee on the constitution of Canada has warned us about the danger which arises as a result of the over-centralization of power in Canada.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when I speak of decentralization as the vehicle to a better society in Canada I do not

August 30, 1973
Adjournment Debate
mean just spreading out some convenient services as if they were some sort of pork barrel. I mean a bold, new concept of government which would recognize that our national unity is dependent on the degree that all Canadians can be close to and participate in their national government. There is no reason the decision makers within certain departments cannot be located in areas other than Ottawa.
Why cannot the agricultural policies be formulated in western Canada; why not the formulation of policies of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in the Atlantic area, with energy policies formulated in Alberta? Why must the head offices of Crown corporations be in Ottawa?
Such positive steps would not only help various regions get their fair share of the economic benefits of federal spending, but the federal process would be enriched by the infusion of creative thinking at the policy-making level. Then the eastern and western provinces would not be just appendages to central Canada's domination of the federal government; they would be active participants.
That is the message of the Western Canada Opportunities Conference, Mr. Speaker, but it is a message the government gave no sign of receiving. I am afraid that the government's half-hearted attempt at decentralization will actually amount to nothing more than sprawling government, in which the departments will add staff on geographic fringes while retaining their decision making apparatus in Ottawa. Without the bold, new concept I have outlined, decentralization will just make a big government bigger and frustrations will multiply.
Let us take advantage of modern communications and transportation to bring government to the people, and true decentralization is the way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Prud'homme (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION-SUGGESTED MOVING OF SOME SERVICES TO ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member is aware, the government favours decentralization of its services, and the matter is under continuous review to ensure that opportunities to this end are taken advantage of fully.
Since last spring, when the hon. member asked what steps the government was taking to decentralize services specifically to western Canada, a number of initiatives have been started. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion announced a major decentralization with the proportion of staff in the capital to be reduced from 70 per cent to 30 per cent.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce began a program to expand the resources and responsibilities of its regional offices, including such initiatives as extending to three new areas the Counselling Assistance to Small Enterprises Program; appointing regional tourist officers in each province, and delegating on an experimental basis to regional offices the granting authority under programs such as the Advancement of Industrial Technology, the General Adjustment Assistance Program, the Program to Enhance Productivity and the Industrial Design Assistance Program.
The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is setting up a number of consumer help offices at the community level, and Information Canada is expanding its

system of regional enquiry centres. The Department of the Environment is developing extensive marine geoscience facilities as part of the new oceanographic institute at Patricia Bay. The National Film Board is opening a Prairie regional production centre.
In addition, consideration is being given to relocating the Science Council out of the National Capital Region, and establishing on the Prairies a new defence research laboratory and a new communications systems engineering facility. The extension of the mint in Winnipeg is well known.
Finally, for perspective, it is worth remembering that as of September last year 207,000 of the 277,000 public servants, or 75 per cent, were employed outside the National Capital Region.
Among this group are included such agencies as the research centres of the Department of the Environment at Burlington, Bedford and Winnipeg, the regional production centres of the National Film Board in Vancouver and Halifax, the Transportation Development Agency in Montreal, the Atmospheric Management Headquarters of DOE in Toronto, and the headquarters of such major Crown corporations as CNR and Air Canada. In other words I would reply to the hon. member that the process of decentralization of the public service is a continuing one and concrete progress is being made. I hope the hon. member will continue pressing the government to decentralize not only, as he said, the offices but also the decision-making power.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-FEED GRAINS-REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF POLICY
AGRICULTURE-FEED GRAINS-REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I refer to a question I asked on July 23. At that time, addressing a question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), in charge of the Wheat Board I asked if he would tell the House what his policy was in respect of the marketing of feed grain since he repeatedly had said there would be changes. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) replied that this minister is responsible and that any stand he takes would be a responsible one. Tonight in these few minutes I wish to call to the attention of the House the deterioration which has taken place in the orderly marketing of feed grain, barley, wheat and oats, from western Canada and call to the attention of the House the concern that has been expressed in western Canada.
I want to point out to the House that the Minister of Agriculture for Manitoba has stated that although the Minister of Justice in charge of the Wheat Board set September 15 as the date for the new policy to come into effect, right now the Canadian Wheat Board is selling No. 1 feed barley at $2.20 per bushel to eastern Canada while the export price is $3.20 per bushel. This statement was made by Mr. Uskiw, the Minister of Agriculture for Manitoba, on August 24. He states that for every bushel that is sold to eastern Canada the prairie grain farmers lose $1. This is the situation at which we are looking. At this point in time we have no indication of what the
August 30,1973

regulations or Orders-in-Council will be as of September 15, although this is the date upon which the Minister in charge of the Wheat Board said the new policy would come into effect.
Now we find the market disorganized. In a wire to the provincial ministers the Minister of Justice said he was working toward stabilization of marketing policy. We had a stable marketing policy until the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and the Minister of Agriculture mucked it up. We had a stable policy, and now we have an unstable and disorganized market.
One might look at the record and see that officials of the federal Department of Agriculture met the representatives of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. When the meeting was over the Minister of Justice from Ottawa, who had not even attended the meeting, said they could like it or lump it. Out of that meeting emerged the representatives of the two governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan saying that the farmers of western Canada would no longer be well served.
If we move from marketing through the Canadian Wheat Board to commodity exchanges in Winnipeg, according to a story put out on August 30 there is a statement to the effect that the commodity market in Winnipeg, the futures market, is no longer in operation. The situation has deteriorated to the extent that there is no regular market pricing system for feed grains being sold in western Canada.
At one time the price of western barley was competitive with the price of United States corn. This is no longer the situation. The ministers responsible said they would set up a pricing policy in eastern Canada comparable to or based on the feed mill price in western Canada, but the feedmill price in western Canada is unknown.
The government has thrown the marketing of feed grains from western Canada into complete disarray. Stability is a thing of the past according to the wheat pool budget of July 20, and I suggest that the government read it. The western farmers are subsidizing the livestock industry in eastern Canada. This is the situation in which they find themselves.
I disagree with those to my right who said this evening that this matter is not of importance. This matter is of importance because it involves not only the well being of the farmer in western and eastern Canada but the unity of this country, and the basis upon which we can do business and have a good understanding of how to carry on business. I can only deplore the lack of information and clear policy of the government which should have been provided by the two ministers who are responsible for agriculture.
I plead with the ministers that if they have anything in mind other than total disorganization, if they have anything in mind which would be to the benefit of Canadian farmers, let them make a statement, either here or elsewhere, on what their policy is so that some kind of an orderly marketing system can be adopted because at present there is a disorganization. They have destroyed the stability of the Canadian Wheat Board. At a time when grains are in short supply and when, above all
Adjournment Debate
things, we need an orderly market they have chosen to disrupt and disorganize what was a stable marketing system.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-RE-EXAMINATION OF REQUIREMENT FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF RURAL ROUTES IN WESTERN CANADA
POST OFFICE-RE-EXAMINATION OF REQUIREMENT FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF RURAL ROUTES IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 12 last I asked a question of the minister in charge of the Post Office in respect of the extension of rural services. In the past few years we have witnessed a phenomenon that has been commonly referred to as rural depopulation. Rural depopulation, I suppose, has been due to various reasons and causes, but one contributing factor which no one denies has been the lack of government services in rural areas, whether they be municipal, provincial or federal. Services which are taken for granted in small towns are often not available in the rural area or if they are, are only available on a limited basis and are often of a second quality.
In recent years decreasing rural population has resulted in the closing of many rural post offices. Some were very, very small indeed and it was not economically feasible to keep them open. However, the government clearly came up with a policy which stated that despite the closure of these small post offices the areas would have postal service better than that being provided through the rural route system. What has happened since that time? The delay in mail deliveries has become almost a national catastrophe. A letter sent on a Wednesday in a so-called remote area will not be delivered perhaps until the next Tuesday. That is not an efficient postal service, Mr. Speaker.
There is also a formula devised by the post office according to which a certain number of people must live along a rural route in order for the service to be extended. In my riding there are areas where the rural route ends, but had it been extended for another mile, three or four more people could have been serviced. The formula does not allow this to be done, and so the truck turns around and retraces the distance already covered. This has created hardship and has forced many people to travel to post

August 30, 1973
Adjournment Debate
offices, sometimes nine or ten miles each way, where apparently they get service.
On April 12 I asked that the government live up to its commitment to review rural routes, and asked that the routes be extended despite the fact that a contract had been signed with a carrier. An additional payment could be made to carriers if the routes were extended to give the service that was promised when the post offices were closed.
Sometimes the post office officials will claim that they cannot extend the rural route for another mile because there are not enough people, but they offer to put a box in the middle of the country where there are large farms and allow the mail to be delivered there. That is not an adequate service, having the mail delivered two or three miles away from a farm, and left there unsupervised. If the mail is delivered mid day, sometimes the people do not only have a chance to pick it up until the end of the day.
We are asking the post office to establish a system to extend the rural routes even during the time of the contracts with the carriers in order to provide service. In many cases the post office is the only regular federal government service that rural people see. They are taxpayers and are entitled to the service.
I submit to the government and to the post office that it is time for more flexibility, without all the bureaucratic redtape and formulae, to be applied to the extension of rural routes.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Leopold Corriveau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: POST OFFICE-RE-EXAMINATION OF REQUIREMENT FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF RURAL ROUTES IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer the question of the hon. member.
According to the last figures available, there were 5,014 rural routes in operation in Canada serving a total of
808,000	households. The criteria for the frequency of the service on those routes are now based on the number of households per mile travelled. When there are more than three households per mile travelled, the mail will then be delivered six times a week. When there are between two and three households per mile, the mail service will be provided four times a week.
Under the current regulations of the department, 4,420 out of the 5,014 rural routes are served six times a week. This means that 88 per cent of the rural routes have a more frequent service than that available to urban users. It is true that most of the routes which are not so well served are in the Prairies because of the continuous increase in the size of the average farm and of the generalized tendency among farmers to move to town or to travel frequently to their farms.
In spite of a less frequent postal service in most of those routes in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, its cost per household is 36 p. 100 above the national average.
If the department decided to give a six day a week service in all of these routes instead of the present four day at least it would cost $1,450,000 more per year. Therefore, the Post Office Department is trying to find other means to determine the frequency of the service.
